catalog_quote: [p.164, §2.1.3] Words in Kontoi, as well as Shinman and Samtao, are monosyllabic, compounds of monosyllables, or single syllables with presyllables. ... [p.168, §2.3.3] The presyllables in Samtao are very similar to those in the other languages. They consist mostly of /p, t, k, s/ with [ə], /ʔa/ and /sɪ/. A few other combinations occur as well but rarely. As with the others, syllabic nasals can also be presyllables. [§2.3.4] There are two tones in Samtao, high and low. Rising and falling do not appear to be significant in Samtao. ... [p.205, §5.2] As was mentioned in section 2, presyllables are unstable and limited in their components. They are non-tonal and unstressed. The CV type presyllables will be discussed first. The vowel in CV type presyllables is generally reduced to [ə].

new_statements.rule_in_words: Samtao words are monosyllables, compounds of monosyllables, or sesquisyllables (presyllable + main syllable). Presyllables (Cə-, ʔa-, si-, syllabic nasal) are unstressed and toneless; stress and the two contrastive tones (high vs. low, with clear/breathy register) belong to the main syllable, i.e. the final syllable of a sesquisyllabic word. Equivalent to fixed main-/final-syllable stress within the phonological word; Paulsen also notes (p.206) that Samtao is losing its presyllables, so many cognates are now plain monosyllables.
new_statements.exceptions: p.178: the word 'with' (item 536) 'is never found in isolation and is never stressed' (a clitic); no statement about stress in compounds of monosyllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical word (wordlist items in citation form, elicited 1986-87 from one Samtao woman from the Samtao mountains north of Kengtung, Shan State, living in Baan Huay Nam Khun, Thailand). The stress remark (p.205) is made for the three languages of the comparison (Kontoi Plang, Shinman Plang, Samtao) jointly, in the reconstruction section, not in a Samtao-specific suprasegmental section.
new_statements.identity_note: Two different things have been called 'Samtao/Samtau'. (1) Paulsen 1992's Samtao = the language of the Samtao mountains north-east of Kengtung, Shan State, Myanmar, whose speakers 'also refer to themselves as Wa' (p.161); her informant was from that area and living among Plang in Baan Huay Nam Khun, Thailand (1986-87); Hopple & Paulsen 1988 call the variety 'Samtao (Pangloh)'. Paulsen states it is mutually unintelligible with Plang. This is the samt1238 [stu] Samtao and is the variety the quoted statement describes. (2) The 'Samtau' of Diffloth 1980 (1976 Harris/Gainey tape) and Diffloth 1979 'Pulang (Samtao)' is, by Diffloth's own later account (1992: 35-36) and Paulsen's (1992: 161), Plang (self-name /plaŋ/, Man Beek dialect) = Blang blan1242. Harper 2009: 7-8 reverses this and says Paulsen's Samtao data are Man Beek, which contradicts Paulsen's own text. Glottolog gives alt names Angku/Āng-kú, Samtau, Samtuan and countries CN, LA, MM, TH; the RWAAI archive files the Laos (Proschan) Samtao recordings under Angkuic, so the Lao 'Samtao' may not be the same variety as Paulsen's.

sources.citation: Harper, Jerod. 2009. Phonological descriptions of Plang spoken in Man Noi, La Gang, and Bang Deng villages (in China). MA thesis, Payap University.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Describes Plang [blan1242], not Samtao; Samtao appears only in the literature review (pp.7-8: Paulsen's reconstruction used Kontoi, Xin Man E and Samtao; Harper claims Paulsen's Samtao 'is actually the Man Beek dialect', which contradicts Paulsen 1992:161). Its own stress statement (sesquisyllables = unstressed presyllable + stressed main syllable) is for Plang.
Bibliographic only: alternative names Angku, Samtau, Samtuan, Āng-kú; countries CN, LA, MM, TH; subclassification comment cites Sidwell 2015: 207.

sources.note: Comparative; 'Samtau' data = 1976 Harris/Gainey tape of a speaker from NE of Keng Tung (p.7), which Paulsen 1992 and Diffloth 1992 later identify as Plang (Man Beek). No stress rule stated; only incidental remarks: two-stop initials are 'separated by an epenthetic unstressed vowel' and the Samtau branch has such initials only with k- (scan p. pg-084 ≈ printed p.85); Samtau has 'a simple two-tone system' (p.23).
